catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic in Bola. It normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word, and hence stress shifts when the root is suffixed with, for instance, a possessive suffix. manu ['mɑnu] ‘fish’ ravulu [rɑ'βulu] ‘ten’ ngatavine [ŋɑtɑ'βinɛ] ‘woman’ bua ['buɑ] ‘heart’ buagu [bu'ɑɡu] ‘my heart’ tabele [tɑ'bɛlɛ] ‘tongue’ tabelena [tɑbɛ'lɛnɑ] ‘his/her/its tongue’ In case the vowel sequences au, ai, ae and oi occur in the antepenultimate and the penultimate syllable of the word, stress shifts to the antepenult. In each of these cases the antepenultimate vowel is lower. Some examples: Bauto ['bɑutɔ] ‘clan name’ mairi ['mɑiri] ‘red clay’ maea ['mɑɛɑ] ‘like this’ oio ['ɔiɔ] ‘oh!’ [§2.5, p. 33] ... [OPD p. 3] Stress is not phonemic. Stress is predictable and occurs penultimately. It is realized by loudness and lengthening. ‘manu ‘fish’ ra’vulu ‘ten’ ngata’vine ‘woman’

new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic in Bola. It normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word, and hence stress shifts when the root is suffixed with, for instance, a possessive suffix. manu ['mɑnu] 'fish' / ravulu [rɑ'βulu] 'ten' / ngatavine [ŋɑtɑ'βinɛ] 'woman' / bua ['buɑ] 'heart' / buagu [bu'ɑɡu] 'my heart' / tabele [tɑ'bɛlɛ] 'tongue' / tabelena [tɑbɛ'lɛnɑ] 'his/her/its tongue'. In case the vowel sequences au, ai, ae and oi occur in the antepenultimate and the penultimate syllable of the word, stress shifts to the antepenult. In each of these cases the antepenultimate vowel is lower. Some examples: Bauto ['bɑutɔ] 'clan name' / mairi ['mɑiri] 'red clay' / maea ['mɑɛɑ] 'like this' / oio ['ɔiɔ] 'oh!'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress on the penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word; possessive and other suffixes move the stress rightward so it stays penultimate. Where a falling-sonority vowel sequence (au, ai, ae, oi) straddles the antepenult and penult, stress lands on the antepenult, i.e. on the lower first vowel of the sequence — equivalently, such sequences behave as one syllable. The 2004 OPD gives the same rule ('predictable and occurs penultimately', realized by loudness and lengthening).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The grammar (§2.4) notes that reduplicated CVV forms such as va va 'four each' ['βɑ: 'βɑ:] carry two stresses on two long syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) CVV roots like ta 'speak', va 'four', ru 'put' are analysed as disyllabic with two identical vowels, so va-ta 'converse' is [βɑ'tɑ:] and ni gi ru 'will be put' [niɡi'ru:] — surface final stress on the long vowel, consistent with penultimate placement under the disyllabic analysis (§2.4, pp. 32-33). (2) kapo 'short' [kɑ'pɔ:] with final long stressed vowel vs kapo ['kɑpɔ] 'to wrap' — explicitly called an exception (§2.4, p. 33, fn. 2). (3) mara 'here it is / behold' 'has irregular stress on the second syllable' (demonstratives section). (4) The 2004 OPD flags that trisyllabic words beginning with the voiced velar fricative + /a/ 'seem to be stressed on that syllable' and that stress on a-initial words 'needs to be checked' (p. 3). (5) Possessive suffix -ne shifts stress (mata-ne 'his eye' [mɑ'tɑnɛ]) but the homophonous preposition ne does not (p. 103); enclitic pronouns and 3S -a also affect stress placement (§2.6).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes (stress shifts under suffixation); enclitic object pronouns (=iau, =ioe) attach with vowel deletion and the grammar notes stress differences between suffix and preposition readings, so the domain is the suffixed word/prosodic word rather than the phrase. Forms are citation/isolation forms with IPA; the OPD adds that stress is realized by loudness and lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe the main Bola language of the Willaumez Peninsula (bola1250); the grammar (§1.4) says Bola has no discernible dialects apart from Harua (Karua/Xarua/Garua/Mai, 3 villages east of Kimbe, ~61-77% lexical similarity), which is not the variety described. The OPD header lists the language as "Bola (Bola-Bakovi) [BNP]".

new_statements.quote: Stress is not phonemic. Stress is predictable and occurs penultimately. It is realized by loudness and lengthening. ‘manu ‘fish’ / ra’vulu ‘ten’ / ngata’vine ‘woman’ / We need to check out stress on words beginning with a. It seems that three syllable words beginning with the voiced velar fricative followed by an /a/ are stressed on that syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate stress = penultimate) and as the existing statement from van den Berg & Wiebe 2019 §2.5 ("Stress is not phonemic in Bola. It normally occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word"), which uses the same three examples (manu, ravulu, ngatavine). The OPD adds the phonetic correlates (loudness and lengthening) and a flagged open question about initial stress in trisyllables beginning with the velar fricative + /a/; the 2019 grammar does not repeat that note and instead formalises the only exception as a shift to the antepenult when the vowel sequences au, ai, ae, oi span the antepenult and penult (Bauto ['bɑutɔ], mairi ['mɑiri], maea ['mɑɛɑ], oi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic and fully predictable: it falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (manu 'MA-nu', ravulu 'ra-VU-lu', ngatavine 'nga-ta-VI-ne') and is realized phonetically by loudness and vowel lengthening.
new_statements.exceptions: A tentative, explicitly unverified note ("We need to check out stress on words beginning with a"): trisyllabic words beginning with the voiced velar fricative (orthographic h, /ɣ/) plus /a/ seem to be stressed on that initial syllable. The example line that follows is garbled in the PDF text ("‘ni, ’ru, nitu, teln"), so no usable examples of the exception survive. No statement on stress in vowel sequences beyond the general remark (p. 2) that certain vowel sequences combine into one syllable when followed by another syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD names the language "Bola (Bola-Bakovi) Language [BNP]", East New Britain & West New Britain Province, with data from Brent Wiebe's four years in the language (checked 27 May 1997); no dialect is specified. Glottolog lists the work as Anonymous 2004, but the PDF itself credits Brent Wiebe, and the 2019 grammar cites it as Wiebe & Wiebe 2000 (its bibliography also lists Wiebe 1995 manuscript). The 2019 grammar notes (citing Wiebe and Wiebe 1998:1) that Harua seems to be a dialect of Bola; neither source states which variety the stress data come from.
